---
title: "Mutational signatures: the concepts behind the package"
---

Mutational signature analysis starts from a simple observation: different
mutational processes leave different imprints in a tumor genome. Ultraviolet
light, APOBEC editing, defective DNA mismatch repair, tobacco smoke -- each
process produces a characteristic pattern of mutations. When many samples are
summarized and decomposed, a small number of recurring patterns emerges, and
those patterns are what the field calls *mutational signatures*
(Alexandrov et al. 2013; the current reference catalog is COSMIC v3.x,
Alexandrov et al. 2020). This page explains the concepts msuiter is built
around. If you already know the domain, skip to
[Get started](get-started.html); every concept here has a hands-on
counterpart in the workflow guides.

## Mutations are counted, not read

The analysis never looks at raw alignments. Variant calls are first converted
into a **catalog of mutations**: a count vector that tallies each mutation
into one of a fixed set of **channels**. A channel is a mutation class --
for single-base substitutions, the channel is the six substitution types
expanded by the bases flanking the mutated one, giving the familiar 96
channel layout. Counting into channels throws away everything except the
pattern, which is exactly what makes patterns comparable across samples and
studies.

msuiter carries five channel systems, because mutational processes leave
imprints at different scales of genome structure:

| System | Channels | Reads from | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| SBS | 96, 192, 384, 1536 | variant calls | single-base substitutions; the strand-aware layouts (192, 384) add transcription-strand context |
| DBS | 78 | variant calls | adjacent doublet substitutions |
| ID | 83 | variant calls | small insertions and deletions |
| CN | 48 | segment tables | copy-number states (total and allele-specific) per length bin |
| SV | 32 | structural-variant records | rearrangement classes (deletions, tandem duplications, inversions, translocations) |

The layouts follow the conventions set by SigProfilerMatrixGenerator
(Bergstrom et al. 2019) and are produced by the Rust tally kernels, so the
same input always produces the same catalog bytes -- the tallies are
reproducible down to the integers.

## Signatures, exposures, and the two directions of analysis

A **signature** is a profile over channels: for each channel, the fraction of
mutations it contributes. The working model is that every sample's catalog is
a mixture -- a set of signatures, each with a sample-specific weight, called
the **exposure**. This gives the two directions the package is named for:

- **Extraction** (de novo): given catalogs, find the signatures and
  exposures that reconstruct them -- a nonnegative matrix factorization
  problem, with the rank (how many signatures) chosen by evidence rather
  than by eye. See [Extracting signatures](signature-extraction.html).
- **Fitting** (assignment): given a known signature set -- for example the
  COSMIC reference catalog shipped in the package -- solve for the exposures
  that best explain each sample, with calibrated uncertainty. See
  [Fitting signatures](signature-fitting.html).

Between the two sit the comparisons: how similar are two signatures or two
catalogs, under a protocol with defined metrics (cosine, and protocol-based
comparisons such as the Hungarian-style assignment used against reference
sets). See [Comparing signatures](comparing-signatures.html).

## The reference data rides with the package

The package bundles the COSMIC v3.6 reference signatures for SBS, DBS and ID
in both GRCh37 and GRCh38 builds under `inst/reference/refdb/`, together with
a manifest. The reference database has its own governance face
(`ms_refdb()`), and the package can tell you whether the bundled catalog is
current for your purposes through the catalog-currency family. You never
need to download reference data to fit against COSMIC signatures.

## Where the statistical discipline comes in

Two questions dominate real analyses, and both are statistical rather than
computational. First, *how many signatures are really there* -- rank
selection -- which msuiter treats as an arbitration problem with cross-
validation evidence, stability vetoes and a diagnostic ladder, not a single
scree-chart eyeball. Second, *which signatures does this sample actually
have* -- assignment under uncertainty, with calibrated coverage rather than
point estimates alone. These two faces, `ms_select_k()` and the MSU-Fit
calibration layer, are the part of the package this project considers its
own contribution; the [capability matrix](capability-matrix.html) states
exactly which claims are backed by which committed evidence.

## Further reading

The concepts on this page are expanded, with runnable sigminer examples, in
the *sigminer book* by the same author
(<https://shixiangwang.github.io/sigminer-book/>); Part 1 there covers the
same taxonomy from the R user's seat, and parts of the presentation above
were adapted from it. The primary literature: Alexandrov et al., *Cell
Reports* 2013 (the signature-decomposition framework); Alexandrov et al.,
*Nature* 2020 (the reference catalog and its rationale); Degasperi et al.,
*Nature Cancer* 2020 (a practical framework and the free-text-to-channel
mapping conventions); Bergstrom et al., *BMC Genomics* 2019
(SigProfilerMatrixGenerator, the channel-layout convention msuiter's SBS/DBS
tallies follow). The copy-number signature model follows Macintyre et al.,
*Nature Genetics* 2018.
